scenes.name: Joy Division
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: De Warsaw, rock pesado con influencias punk, a la desolación ballardiana: la originalidad crece a medida que las canciones se vuelven lentas y ralas, con el bajo de Peter Hook llevando la melodía, la guitarra de Bernard Sumner abriendo huecos, la batería de Stephen Morris rodeando un cráter y Ian Curtis recitando desde «un lugar solitario». Martin Hannett, productor de Factory, convierte el espacio en «control atmosférico» con delays digitales y grabaciones separadas: Unknown Pleasures (1979), con la portada del púlsar de Peter Saville, «Transmission», «Atmosphere». El coqueteo con la imaginería nazi, la epilepsia, los barbitúricos y un matrimonio roto desembocan en Closer, «estar dentro de la cabeza de Curtis», y en su suicidio en mayo de 1980. «Love Will Tear Us Apart» es su primer hit. Los supervivientes empiezan de cero como New Order.

scenes.name: New Order
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Los supervivientes de Joy Division, perdidos tras la muerte de Curtis («Ceremony», Movement), echan a Martin Hannett, aprenden a programar cajas de ritmos con música electrónica italiana y descubren en Nueva York los clubes chic, la emisora Kiss FM, los remixes de Pettibone, el freestyle y el electro. «Everything's Gone Green» (1981) marca el giro; «Blue Monday» (1983) y «Confusion», producido por Arthur Baker, los convierten en una banda de baile. Con Factory abren The Haçienda, inspirada en Danceteria y Funhouse.

scenes.name: 808 State
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: Formados en 1988 en la tienda Eastern Bloc de Martin Price por Graham Massey (ex Biting Tongues) y Gerald Simpson, que grababan como Hit Squad, uno de tantos grupos británicos de hip hop que abrazaron el acid house. El EP Newbuild (1988) era un acid más directo y siniestro que el de Londres; tras «Pacific State» (Quadrastate, 1989) Simpson se fue por una disputa de pagos y entraron Darren Partington y Andy Barker: «un equipo de producción que en el escenario parece un grupo». Tommy Boy los fichó en 1990 y en Estados Unidos los vendió como grupo alternativo, junto a bandas de guitarras. «Donkey Doctor» (808:90) cita «Techno City» de Cybotron; Ex:El (1991) trajo a Bernard Sumner («Spanish Heart») y a una Björk todavía de los Sugarcubes («Ooops»), escándalo para los puristas. Partington recuerda que el público americano te exige «¡entretenme!».

podcast.title: Sequencing Bass Line Idea
podcast.body: Bernard Sumner, the singer for New Order, originated the idea of sequencing a bass line from Peter Hook. This concept was pivotal in establishing the foundations of a new song played entirely by machines, influencing the band's future electronic direction. "It was singer Bernard Sumner who came up with the idea of sequencing a line in from bass player Peter Hook."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Musical Evolution (1982)
xref.body: Initially, New Order sounded similar to Joy Division. However, a trip to New York, where they were exposed to post-disco, early house, and electro music, changed their direction. They became fascinated with synthesizers, drum machines, and sequencers, shifting by 1982 from Joy Division's guitar-based style to a more electronic and dance-oriented sound with Bernard Sumner fronting the band. "And by 1982, New Order had moved away from the guitar-based material that Joy Division had become famous for into something more electronic and dancing, all with Bernard out front."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Blue Monday (1983) – Band Agreed to Dissolve if Anyone Left; Reconstituted as New Order After Ian Curtis's Death

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Accident of Laziness" Origin of Dance Sound
xref.body: New Order's groundbreaking electronic sound and worldwide alt-rock influence partly originated from their reluctance to perform encores. They initially played Stephen Morris's drum machine alone as they left the stage, later adding a sequencer for Gillian Gilbert's synthesizers, and finally, Bernard Sumner conceived sequencing Peter Hook's bass line, leading to songs performed largely by machines. "But their worldwide success and the way they changed alt rock forever was due to an accident of laziness."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bernard Sumner as Lead Singer
xref.body: During rehearsals, each member took a turn on lead vocals, with Bernard Sumner ultimately taking on the role. He had to learn to sing and play guitar simultaneously. "And in the end, it was Bernard Sumner. He just had to learn to sing and play guitar at the same time, something that he had to do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

xref.title: Diverse Musical Inspirations
xref.body: His inspirations include Jimi Hendrix, Joe Strummer, Captain Beefheart, Frank Zappa, Robert Johnson, Bernard Sumner of New Order, and significantly, John McGeoch of Siouxsie and the Banshees, admired for his varied soundscapes. "And who does he look for for inspiration? Well, we talked about Hendrix, but also Joe Strummer, Captain B. Fart, Frank Zappa, loose legend Robert Johnson, Bernard Sumner of New Order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Name Origin
xref.body: After Ian Curtis's death, surviving Joy Division members Bernard Sumner, Peter Hook, and Stephen Morris discussed their future. Encouraged by their progress as Joy Division, they decided to move forward under a new name. Their manager, Rob Gretton, suggested "New Order" after finding the phrase in a newspaper headline about mass killings in Pol Pot's Cambodia. "Their manager, my name Rob Greten, is the one who came up with it. He found the name in a newspaper headline about the mass killings in Pol Potts, Cambodia. The phrase was new order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

xref.title: Inspiration for John Frusciante
xref.body: Bernard Sumner is cited as one of John Frusciante's sources of inspiration. "Bernard Sumner of New Order."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Longevity
xref.body: New Order continues to be active today, with Bernard Sumner still serving as the band's singer. "And New Order is still with us today, and Bernard Sumner is still singing for the band today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sequenced Bass Line
xref.body: Peter Hook's bass line was sequenced by Bernard Sumner for a new song, contributing a fundamental element to New Order's innovative machine-driven sound. "sequencing a line in from bass player Peter Hook."
